story.head: Tilted ice, toward the Predators’ net
paras: The Senators won the teams’ first meeting this season, 3-2 in a shootout in Ottawa on Oct 10. The Senators (17-7-3) beat Tampa Bay 6-2 on Friday, while the Predators (13-6-6) lost 6-5 in a shootout to Utah the same night. Going in, the Sens are first in the Atlantic (fourth in the NHL) and the Predators third in the Central (tied for ninth).

The Senators’ record (.685) is running ahead of what their chances are worth (.615), largely because they’re 8-3 in one-goal games. So is the Predators’ (.640 on chances worth .526), largely thanks to pulling off wins in one-goal games.

The Senators rarely get pinned in their own end (2nd), keep dangerous shots away better than almost anyone (3rd) and get into a lot of chippy games (3rd). The Predators, by contrast, get pinned in their own end on long shifts (30th). They also keep things calm after the whistle (2nd lowest). They also give up a lot of shots (30th), so the Senators keep shots away, but they give up plenty. Put that together and the Senators’ forecheck could keep the Predators pinned in their own end.

Tim Stützle (15 G / 18 A / 33 P in 27 GP) leads the Senators in scoring, with seven points in his last five games. For the Predators, Filip Forsberg (10 G / 17 A / 27 P in 25 GP) leads the way in scoring, and Steven Stamkos (12 G / 12 A / 24 P in 25 GP) has a team-high twelve goals.
Linus Ullmark (13-2-0 / .933 SV% in 15 GS) has been a rock in net for Ottawa and will likely start. Juuse Saros (9-4-5 / .914 SV% in 18 GS) has been outstanding for Nashville and will likely start.

At home, Andrew Brunette likes to send Schaefer, Kerfoot and Marchessault out against opponents’ fourth lines, so watch for them against Burakovsky, Halliday and Cousins. One more thing: the Senators usually control more of the chances than the Predators do.
